blocks.c: Oskar Schindler (Liam Neeson) holds an object and looks distraught in Schindler's List (1993).

blocks.x: Schindler's List follows the gradual change in a man who begins by exploiting the system and eventually uses his money, contacts, and factory to keep people alive inside it. Oskar Schindler (Liam Neeson) arrives in Nazi-occupied Kraków as a businessman looking to profit from the war, opening a factory staffed largely by Jewish workers because the labor is cheap.

What destroys me is how late Schindler realizes that survival cannot be measured cleanly. He has already saved more than a thousand people when he breaks down over the car he could have sold, the pin he could have traded, the possibility that one more person might have lived. Itzhak Stern (Ben Kingsley) tries to tell him what he did accomplish, but Schindler can only see the people he did not reach. That scene refuses triumph. The real release comes later, when the surviving Schindler Jews and their descendants place stones on his grave. The movie finally lets history answer him. He thought it was not enough. For generations of people who existed because of what he did, it was everything.
